card.title: Work Done by a Constant Force and a Variable Force

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Work is the energy a force transfers along a displacement: $W = \vec F\cdot\vec s = Fs\cos\theta$ — a scalar, zero for perpendicular forces, negative for friction. Work by a **variable force** integrates: $W = \int F\,dx$, read as the area under the force–displacement graph; the spring is the standard case, $W = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$ — stretching k = 200 N/m by 0.1 m stores 1 J (NEB 2024).…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - W = Fs cos θ - Variable force: W = ∫F dx - Spring: W = ½kx² - P = W/t

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Dot Product: W = F·d·cosθ — only force component parallel to displacement does work.  ·  Variable Force Integration: Must integrate F(x)·dx; cannot use W = Fd unless F constant.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "No displacement, no work — no matter how hard you push."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Spring stretch*** — ½kx² with k = 200 N/m, x = 0.1 m gives 1 J (NEB 2024).

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **Work vs energy:** work is energy in transit (a process); energy is the capacity (a state) — both measured in joules.  ·  **Zero work cases:** force perpendicular to displacement (circular motion) or zero displacement (pushing a wall) — no transfer either way.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Force That Transfers Energy Work is force's energy invoice: $W = \vec F\cdot\vec s$. Pushing a wall does no work; lifting a bucket does. This topic covers work by constant and variable forces, the spring as the standard variable-force example, and the definitions of work, energy and power (NEB 2021).  ·  ## 2. rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "Perpendicular force does zero work; spring work is half k x squared."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Numerical (3m): A 20 kg crate is dragged 10 m by a 50 N force at 60° above the horizontal. Find the work done by the force.** — W = Fs cos θ = 50 × 10 × cos 60° = 250 J; only the horizontal 25 N component acts along the motion.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Most-tested: spring numerical (2024) and the definition triplet (2021). Area under F–x graphs is the variable-force tool.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Only the force component along displacement works:** the cos θ factor prices every push.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: W = F⃗·s⃗ = Fs cos θ — scalar; joule = N·m.  ·  Variable force: W = ∫F dx = area under F–x graph.  ·  Spring: W = ½kx² (200 N/m stretched 0.1 m → 1 J).

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The joule is a derived unit: 1 J = 1 kg·m²/s² — energy's dimensions are mass × velocity².
